In Experiment 1 (n = 99; Mage = 10.48 ± 0.86 years), children were randomly assigned to Moral Elevation, Joy, or Neutral groups. Psychophysiological measures were recorded during both the baseline and task phases, while self-reported prosocial behavior was assessed using validated scales. Participants in the Moral Elevation group experienced emotional states marked by inspired, moved, touched, admiration, and uplifted, accompanied by a distinct pattern of sympathetic-parasympathetic coactivation. Although not statistically significant in self-reported measures, a notable pattern emerged wherein Moral Elevation yielded the highest prosocial scores, followed by Joy and then Neutral conditions. Experiment 2 (n = 92; Mage = 10.84 ± 0.76 years) employed a single-category Implicit Association Test (IAT) to assess prosocial behavioral tendencies. The Moral Elevation group exhibited a significantly stronger implicit prosocial bias on the IAT compared to both Joy and Neutral groups. These findings suggest that moral elevation possesses a unique emotional profile separate from general positive affect that activates dual dissociable pathways for children's prosocial behavior: explicit and implicit processes. The study provides empirical support for incorporating moral elevation interventions in educational settings to cultivate integrated prosocial development.

papers.title: Types of moral values found in yesterday movie
papers.abstract: Moral values are concepts that serve as a guideline on implementing our manners, personalities, and behaviors toward ourselves and others. The movie is one of the best platforms to deliver moral values, it makes this study needed because it was found a lot of movie’s viewers only focused on fun things that existed in the movie than focused on the moral messages conveyed in it. The aim of this study is to tell the readers what moral values are, and the types of moral values, and help people in recognizing moral values that appear in the movie. This study used a descriptive qualitative method in analyzing the data and a documentation method used in collecting the data. As a result, there were eleven types of moral values that appeared in Yesterday movie, consisting of honesty, bravery, peace ability, confidence, purity & pureness, loyalty, respect, love & affection, sensitivity & selflessness, kind & friendly, and fair & humane. This finding shows that this comedy movie has many moral values to present.

papers.title: Probing Pre-Trained Language Models for Cross-Cultural Differences in Values
papers.research_question: Do pre-trained language models capture cross-cultural differences in values, and do these align with established values surveys?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-trained language models capture cross-cultural differences in values, but these differences only weakly align with established values surveys.
papers.conclusion: PLMs capture marked differences in values between cultures, though these are only weakly correlated with values surveys.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs capture marked differences in cultural values across different languages and countries.
There is low agreement in value predictions between different multilingual PLMs (mBERT, XLM, XLM-R).
The values embedded in PLMs show weak or no significant correlation with established values surveys like Hofstede's and the World Values Survey.
A significant percentage of country pairs show statistically significant differences in model predictions for WVS questions, indicating cross-cultural diversity.
Model design and training choices affect the cultural biases picked up, as seen in differences between models trained on similar data.
papers.limitation:
Probing with cloze-style questions only shows static and extrinsic biases at inference time, not intrinsic measures.
Mapping countries to cultures and languages is imperfect and may misrepresent communities, including minority and diaspora communities.
Surveys are imperfect tools for quantifying cultural disparity, with confounding factors and problems viewing populations as homogeneous.
future_direction: Analysis based on the Inglehart–Welzel cultural map from the World Values Survey.
papers.abstract: Language embeds information about social, cultural, and political values people hold. Prior work has explored potentially harmful social biases encoded in Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs). However, there has been no systematic study investigating how values embedded in these models vary across cultures. In this paper, we introduce probes to study which cross-cultural values are embedded in these models, and whether they align with existing theories and cross-cultural values surveys. We find that PLMs capture differences in values across cultures, but those only weakly align with established values surveys. We discuss implications of using mis-aligned models in cross-cultural settings, as well as ways of aligning PLMs with values surveys.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Emergent Moral Representations in Large Language Models Aligns with Human Conceptual, Neural, and Behavioral Moral Structure
papers.research_question: Do large language models internally encode structured representations of morality that parallel human conceptual, behavioral, and neural organization?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models spontaneously develop dissociable and structured moral representations whose internal geometry parallels human neural and behavioral moral structures, positioning them as emerging neurocognitive models of moral reasoning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs acquire moral representations that parallel human moral cognition, suggesting they can serve as computational models for moral reasoning and value alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Moral foundations are linearly decodable from hidden activations of LLMs, with peak discriminability in mid layers.
The representational geometry of moral foundations in LLMs aligns with human conceptual taxonomies (e.g., Individualizing vs. Binding/Social, Moral vs. Social).
LLM mid-layer activations predict human wrongness judgments.
The posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) in humans shows robust decoding of moral foundations and its representational structure aligns with LLM mid-layer activations.
Partial least squares correlation reveals orthogonal activation dimensions corresponding to individual foundations and higher-order abstractions.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in ethically sensitive settings, yet it remains unclear whether they internally encode structured representations of morality. Here we examine the activation space representations of several mid-sized LLMs to test whether statistical learning over text gives rise to moral distinctions that parallel human conceptual, behavioral, and neural organization. Using multivariate decoding, representational similarity analysis, partial least squares correlation, and behavioral prediction, we show that moral foundations are linearly decodable from hidden activations, with peak discriminability in mid layers. Representational similarity analysis uncovered a hierarchical moral geometry consistent with Moral Foundations Theory, with the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) showing robust multivariate decoding and a representational structure that aligned most strongly with mid-layer LLM activations. These same mid-layers also predicted human wrongness judgments, indicating a shared computational substrate for moral evaluation. Partial least squares correlation further revealed orthogonal activation dimensions corresponding to individual foundations and their higher-order abstractions, yielding interpretable axes along which moral meaning is encoded. These results reveal a striking convergence across conceptual, behavioral, neural, and model representations, positioning LLMs as emerging neurocognitive models of moral reasoning and offering a window into the internal mechanisms that shape their behavior in sensitive domains. Such alignment may enable more explainable and transparent AI systems and support future efforts to ground LLMs in human values.

papers.title: The Straight and Narrow: Do LLMs Possess an Internal Moral Path?
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess an internal moral path, or are they merely capturing superficial linguistic artifacts? The paper investigates the internal moral representations of LLMs and how to manipulate them for safety.
papers.core_contribution: The paper maps Moral Foundations Theory onto the latent space of LLMs, confirming linearly separable moral representations, and introduces Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF) to dynamically steer these representations for safety, effectively balancing the safety-helpfulness trade-off.
papers.conclusion: The work bridges the gap between superficial behavioral guardrails and intrinsic alignment by mapping and manipulating moral representations within LLMs, demonstrating that activation engineering can serve as a robust intrinsic defense mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode linearly separable moral representations in their middle layers, forming a shared yet distinct moral subspace across English and Chinese.
Steerable Moral Vectors can be extracted and causally modulate the model's internal state and behavioral output, shifting responses between 'Virtue' and 'Vice'.
Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF) synergizes probe detection with vector injection, reducing jailbreak success rates on HarmBench while minimizing incorrect refusals on XSTest.
Cross-lingual analysis reveals 'Asymmetric Feature Coverage' where some moral concepts (e.g., Care, Loyalty-Vice) are more richly encoded in Chinese, while others (e.g., Sanctity-Virtue, Authority-Virtue) are more robust in English.
Moral Vector injection reveals implicit correlations between foundations, such as Fairness and Loyalty amplifying Authority-virtue, and identifies Sanctity-vice as a 'universal negative pole'.
papers.limitation:
The cultural and theoretical scope is limited to English and Chinese and grounded solely in Moral Foundations Theory, potentially overlooking other ethical frameworks and low-resource cultures.
The Moral Virtue-Vice dataset was generated by an LLM (Gemini 3 Pro) without large-scale human annotation, potentially reflecting the generator's biases.
Validation was primarily on the Llama-3.1 family; generalizability to other architectures requires further study.
future_direction: Extending the framework to diverse model architectures.
Expanding the cross-lingual analysis to capture a broader spectrum of global cultural morality.
Incorporating ethical frameworks beyond Moral Foundations Theory.
papers.abstract: Enhancing the moral alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical challenge in AI safety. Current alignment techniques often act as superficial guardrails, leaving the intrinsic moral representations of LLMs largely untouched. In this paper, we bridge this gap by leveraging Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) to map and manipulate the fine-grained moral landscape of LLMs. Through cross-lingual linear probing, we validate the shared nature of moral representations in middle layers and uncover a shared yet different moral subspace between English and Chinese. Building upon this, we extract steerable Moral Vectors and successfully validate their efficacy at both internal and behavioral levels. Leveraging the high generalizability of morality, we propose Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF), a dynamic inference-time intervention that synergizes probe detection with vector injection to tackle the safety-helpfulness trade-off. Empirical results confirm that our approach acts as a targeted intrinsic defense, effectively reducing incorrect refusals on benign queries while minimizing jailbreak success rates compared to standard baselines.

papers.title: Exploring and steering the moral compass of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the moral profiles of state-of-the-art LLMs, and can their moral reasoning be steered using activation steering techniques?
papers.core_contribution: Proprietary LLMs are predominantly utilitarian while open-weight LLMs are more deontological, and a novel activation steering method (SARA) can effectively steer models' moral reasoning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess distinct ethical dimensions that reflect their training and design, and activation steering methods like SARA offer a means to intervene and modulate their moral reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Proprietary LLMs align more with utilitarian ethics, whereas open-weight LLMs align more with deontological/value-based ethics.
All models except Llama-2-7B exhibit a strong liberal bias in moral foundations.
Model responses show high variability, with different transition patterns between ethical schools for proprietary vs. open models.
The proposed SARA method reliably steers model responses toward desired ethical directions (e.g., utilitarian or Kantian).
SARA is most effective when intervening on early or late layers, with mid layers yielding mixed results.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become central to advancing automation and decision-making across various sectors, raising significant ethical questions. This study proposes a comprehensive comparative analysis of the most advanced LLMs to assess their moral profiles. We subjected several state-of-the-art models to a selection of ethical dilemmas and found that all the proprietary ones are mostly utilitarian and all of the open-weights ones align mostly with values-based ethics. Furthermore, when using the Moral Foundations Questionnaire, all models we probed - except for Llama 2-7B - displayed a strong liberal bias. Lastly, in order to causally intervene in one of the studied models, we propose a novel similarity-specific activation steering technique. Using this method, we were able to reliably steer the model's moral compass to different ethical schools. All of these results showcase that there is an ethical dimension in already deployed LLMs, an aspect that is generally overlooked.

papers.title: Building Interpretable Models for Moral Decision-Making
papers.research_question: How do neural networks make moral decisions on trolley-style dilemmas, and where do moral biases originate within their architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Designs a 2-layer transformer optimized for moral reasoning tasks, achieving 77% accuracy on Moral Machine data, and combines interpretability methods to map internal mechanisms of moral judgment.
papers.conclusion: Demonstrates that small, custom transformers can achieve moral competence and be transparently analyzed, enabling targeted interventions for bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns a moral hierarchy where characters like Pregnant and Stroller have positive causal effects, while Criminal has negative effects.
Moral biases localize to distinct computational stages: legality bias in Layer 0 and species bias in Layer 1.
Circuit probing identifies sparse subnetworks in the MLP block that causally implement moral scoring.
The model shows functional specialization with different attention heads specializing in different bias dimensions.
Small, custom transformers can achieve moral competence while remaining interpretable, enabling targeted bias interventions.
papers.limitation: Training on aggregate human preferences inherits cultural biases.
future_direction: Extend the approach to traditional large language models on moral questions.
papers.abstract: We build a custom transformer model to study how neural networks make moral decisions on trolley-style dilemmas. The model processes structured scenarios using embeddings that encode who is affected, how many people, and which outcome they belong to. Our 2-layer architecture achieves 77% accuracy on Moral Machine data while remaining small enough for detailed analysis. We use different interpretability techniques to uncover how moral reasoning distributes across the network, demonstrating that biases localize to distinct computational stages among other findings.

papers.title: Do Large GPT Models Discover Moral Dimensions in Language Representations? A Topological Study Of Sentence Embeddings
papers.research_question: Does GPT-3.5 encode moral dimensions, specifically fairness, in its sentence embeddings? The paper uses topological methods to analyze this.
papers.core_contribution: GPT-3.5 develops a moral dimension in its representation space, with topological separation between fair and unfair sentences.
papers.conclusion: GPT-3.5 encodes moral dimensions of fairness in its representation space, and topological analysis offers a novel intrinsic method for AI interpretability and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Sentence embeddings from GPT-3.5 can be decomposed into two submanifolds corresponding to fair and unfair moral judgments.
A fairness metric based on social psychology factors allows projection and visualization of moral dimensions.
The topological method provides an intrinsic way to examine model abilities without relying on behavioral outputs.
The separation indicates that GPT-3.5 induces an understanding of fairness during training.
This approach is novel in AI interpretability and could benefit alignment research.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models are deployed within Artificial Intelligence systems, that are increasingly integrated with human society, it becomes more important than ever to study their internal structures. Higher level abilities of LLMs such as GPT-3.5 emerge in large part due to informative language representations they induce from raw text data during pre-training on trillions of words. These embeddings exist in vector spaces of several thousand dimensions, and their processing involves mapping between multiple vector spaces, with total number of parameters on the order of trillions. Furthermore, these language representations are induced by gradient optimization, resulting in a black box system that is hard to interpret. In this paper, we take a look at the topological structure of neuronal activity in the "brain" of Chat-GPT's foundation language model, and analyze it with respect to a metric representing the notion of fairness. We develop a novel approach to visualize GPT's moral dimensions. We first compute a fairness metric, inspired by social psychology literature, to identify factors that typically influence fairness assessments in humans, such as legitimacy, need, and responsibility. Subsequently, we summarize the manifold's shape using a lower-dimensional simplicial complex, whose topology is derived from this metric. We color it with a heat map associated with this fairness metric, producing human-readable visualizations of the high-dimensional sentence manifold. Our results show that sentence embeddings based on GPT-3.5 can be decomposed into two submanifolds corresponding to fair and unfair moral judgments. This indicates that GPT-based language models develop a moral dimension within their representation spaces and induce an understanding of fairness during their training process.

papers.title: Value Entanglement: Conflation Between Different Kinds of Good In (Some) Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs distinguish three different kinds of good: moral, grammatical, and economic.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit value entanglement, where moral value influences grammatical and economic judgments, and this conflation can be repaired by selective ablation of morality-related activation vectors.
papers.conclusion: Value entanglement exists in some LLMs, particularly open-weight models, and can be mitigated by targeted interventions like ablation.
papers.key_findings:
Grammaticality and morality ratings are correlated in some LLMs (e.g., GPT-3.5, Qwen2.5-7B) but not in humans.
Economic value ratings are influenced by moral context in some LLMs, reducing correlation with ground truth prices.
Embedding models show high correlation between morality and grammaticality vectors, indicating entangled representations.
Residual stream activations show entanglement between moral and grammatical/economic projections across layers.
Directional ablation of moral vectors improves grammatical and economic judgment correlations with human norms.
papers.abstract: Value alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) requires us to empirically measure these models' actual, acquired representation of value. Among the characteristics of value representation in humans is that they distinguish among value of different kinds. We investigate whether LLMs likewise distinguish three different kinds of good: moral, grammatical, and economic. By probing model behavior, embeddings, and residual stream activations, we report pervasive cases of value entanglement: a conflation between these distinct representations of value. Specifically, both grammatical and economic valuation was found to be overly influenced by moral value, relative to human norms. This conflation was repaired by selective ablation of the activation vectors associated with morality.

papers.title: Tracing Moral Foundations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the moral judgment in large language models reflect an internal structured representation of moral concepts, or is it merely superficial mimicry of linguistic patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides mechanistic evidence that moral concepts in LLMs are encoded in a structured, layer-dependent way that aligns with human judgments, and demonstrates causal links through steering interventions.
papers.conclusion: The findings indicate that LLMs develop structured moral geometries, supporting the idea that moral pluralism can arise from statistical learning on language data alone.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs represent moral foundations in a way that aligns with human moral perceptions.
Moral foundations correspond to separable linear axes in the models' representation space.
Sparse autoencoder features decompose moral foundations into interpretable, atomic concepts.
Steering interventions along moral vectors or SAE features causally shift moral judgments.
The structure suggests pluralistic moral representations emerge from language training.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to two instruction-tuned LLMs.
Moral concept vectors derived from English-language vignettes.
Steering interventions are linear and applied at a single layer.
future_direction: Extend approach to more models and languages.
Explore non-linear interventions.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce human-like moral judgments, but it is unclear whether this reflects an internal conceptual structure or superficial ``moral mimicry.'' Using Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) as an analytic framework, we study how moral foundations are encoded, organized, and expressed within two instruction-tuned LLMs: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We employ a multi-level approach combining (i) layer-wise analysis of MFT concept representations and their alignment with human moral perceptions, (ii) pretrained sparse autoencoders (SAEs) over the residual stream to identify sparse features that support moral concepts, and (iii) causal steering interventions using dense MFT vectors and sparse SAE features. We find that both models represent and distinguish moral foundations in a structured, layer-dependent way that aligns with human judgments. At a finer scale, SAE features show clear semantic links to specific foundations, suggesting partially disentangled mechanisms within shared representations. Finally, steering along either dense vectors or sparse features produces predictable shifts in foundation-relevant behavior, demonstrating a causal connection between internal representations and moral outputs. Together, our results provide mechanistic evidence that moral concepts in LLMs are distributed, layered, and partly disentangled, suggesting that pluralistic moral structure can emerge as a latent pattern from the statistical regularities of language alone.

papers.title: Large Pre-trained Language Models Contain Human-like Biases of What is Right and Wrong to Do
papers.research_question: Do large pre-trained language models contain human-like biases of what is right and wrong to do, and can these biases be captured by a geometric direction in the embedding space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that pre-trained language models contain a 'moral direction' in their embedding space, which can be extracted via PCA and used to rate the normativity of phrases and prevent toxic degeneration in language models.
papers.conclusion: Pre-trained language models contain human-like moral biases that can be extracted as a geometric direction, providing a path for attenuating toxic degeneration and aligning language models with human values.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's embedding space contains a moral direction that strongly correlates with human moral judgments.
The moral direction can be used to rate the normativity of arbitrary phrases without explicit training.
The moral direction can guide language models (e.g., GPT-2) to produce normative text and prevent toxic degeneration, outperforming previous approaches.
Contextual information significantly affects human moral judgments, and BERT's moral direction captures this context dependence.
The moral direction reflects societal norms present in the training data, but may be specific to English-speaking cultures of the 21st century.
papers.limitation: BERT was mainly trained on English Books and English Wikipedia, so it may primarily mirror English-speaking cultures of the 21st century.
future_direction: Investigating social or demographic biases in the context of mimicked moral norms.
papers.abstract: Artificial writing is permeating our lives due to recent advances in large-scale, transformer-based language models (LMs) such as BERT, its variants, GPT-2/3, and others. Using them as pre-trained models and fine-tuning them for specific tasks, researchers have extended state of the art for many NLP tasks and shown that they capture not only linguistic knowledge but also retain general knowledge implicitly present in the data. Unfortunately, LMs trained on unfiltered text corpora suffer from degenerated and biased behaviour. While this is well established, we show that recent LMs also contain human-like biases of what is right and wrong to do, some form of ethical and moral norms of the society -- they bring a "moral direction" to surface. That is, we show that these norms can be captured geometrically by a direction, which can be computed, e.g., by a PCA, in the embedding space, reflecting well the agreement of phrases to social norms implicitly expressed in the training texts and providing a path for attenuating or even preventing toxic degeneration in LMs. Being able to rate the (non-)normativity of arbitrary phrases without explicitly training the LM for this task, we demonstrate the capabilities of the "moral direction" for guiding (even other) LMs towards producing normative text and showcase it on RealToxicityPrompts testbed, preventing the neural toxic degeneration in GPT-2.

papers.title: Analysing Moral Bias in Finetuned LLMs through Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (a moral bias in intentionality judgments), whether specific Transformer layers encode this bias, and whether targeted interventions (layer-patching) can mitigate it.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the Knobe effect (a moral bias) emerges in finetuned LLMs, is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, and can be mitigated by patching activations from pretrained models into finetuned models, without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that social biases in LLMs can be mechanistically localized and mitigated through targeted interventions like layer-patching, offering a method for model repair without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Finetuned LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (moral bias in intentionality judgments), while pretrained models show minimal effect.
The bias is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, as shown by differences in residual stream activations.
Patching activations from pretrained models into specific layers of finetuned models can reduce or eliminate the bias.
The mitigation via layer-patching does not significantly harm general model performance on standard benchmarks.
The Knobe effect is not an emergent property of model scale alone; it is induced by finetuning and appears across model sizes.
papers.limitation: The layer-patching method requires access to the pretrained model.
future_direction: Explore whether this localization technique applies to other biases, such as gender or racial stereotypes.
Develop methods that do not rely on access to the pretrained model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to internalize human-like biases during finetuning, yet the mechanisms by which these biases manifest remain unclear. In this work, we investigated whether the well-known Knobe effect, a moral bias in intentionality judgements, emerges in finetuned LLMs and whether it can be traced back to specific components of the model. We conducted a Layer-Patching analysis across 3 open-weights LLMs and demonstrated that the bias is not only learned during finetuning but also localized in a specific set of layers. Surprisingly, we found that patching activations from the corresponding pretrained model into just a few critical layers is sufficient to eliminate the effect. Our findings offer new evidence that social biases in LLMs can be interpreted, localized, and mitigated through targeted interventions, without the need for model retraining.

papers.title: Aligned but Blind: Alignment Increases Implicit Bias by Reducing Awareness of Race
papers.research_question: How does alignment in language models lead to increased implicit bias by reducing awareness of race?
papers.core_contribution: Alignment in language models increases implicit bias by reducing awareness of race in ambiguous contexts, and a mitigation strategy that incentivizes race representation in early layers effectively reduces this bias.
papers.conclusion: Value-aligned LMs exhibit implicit bias in ambiguous contexts due to race blindness, and interventions that increase race awareness can mitigate this bias, highlighting limitations in current alignment methods.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment reduces explicit bias to near zero but significantly increases implicit bias in word association tasks.
Aligned models fail to represent racial concepts in ambiguous contexts, treating polysemous words like 'black' and 'white' as color rather than race.
Activation patching shows that aligned models are less likely to interpret race in ambiguous prompts, indicating race blindness.
Interventions that inject race-laden activations or fine-tune models to associate ambiguous words with race reduce implicit bias.
Early layer interventions are more effective than later layers for bias mitigation.
papers.limitation:
Focused solely on racial biases using the ambiguity of black and white in Llama 3 models.
Mechanistic interpretations are influenced by model architecture, data, and interpretability methods, and are limited by human-defined concepts.
Amplifying race associations may have side effects beyond bias metrics examined.
Qualitative comparisons to human race blindness may not fully capture psychological motivations.
future_direction: Extend the approach to other types of social bias, such as gender bias.
Investigate the origins of the associations between color and concepts in pretraining.
Study more tokens with ambiguity in broader contexts across different model families.
papers.abstract: Although value-aligned language models (LMs) appear unbiased in explicit bias evaluations, they often exhibit stereotypes in implicit word association tasks, raising concerns about their fair usage. We investigate the mechanisms behind this discrepancy and find that alignment surprisingly amplifies implicit bias in model outputs. Specifically, we show that aligned LMs, unlike their unaligned counterparts, overlook racial concepts in early internal representations when the context is ambiguous. Not representing race likely fails to activate safety guardrails, leading to unintended biases. Inspired by this insight, we propose a new bias mitigation strategy that works by incentivizing the representation of racial concepts in the early model layers. In contrast to conventional mitigation methods of machine unlearning, our interventions find that steering the model to be more aware of racial concepts effectively mitigates implicit bias. Similar to race blindness in humans, ignoring racial nuances can inadvertently perpetuate subtle biases in LMs.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: High-Dimension Human Value Representation in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we represent human values in LLMs in a high-dimensional space to understand how LLMs prioritize values across languages and cultures?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces UniVaR, a high-dimensional neural representation of human values in LLMs, which captures value-relevant features and enables visualization of value differences across languages and cultures.
papers.conclusion: UniVaR provides a systematic approach to understanding value systems in LLMs and is a powerful tool for making LLMs more transparent and accountable.
papers.key_findings:
UniVaR achieves significantly higher accuracy than baseline embeddings on the value identification task.
UniVaR captures value-relevant features while minimizing the influence of non-value-related confounders like translation artifacts.
Value representations cluster by language, indicating that LLMs exhibit distinct values across languages.
The value distances between languages reflect cultural similarities (e.g., European languages cluster together, East Asian languages cluster together).
UniVaR can be used to visualize and analyze the value alignment process, as shown in the DPO experiment.
papers.limitation: UniVaR might still be affected by generation and translation artifacts such as writing style and translationese.
papers.abstract: The widespread application of LLMs across various tasks and fields has necessitated the alignment of these models with human values and preferences. Given various approaches of human value alignment, there is an urgent need to understand the scope and nature of human values injected into these LLMs before their deployment and adoption. We propose UniVaR, a high-dimensional neural representation of symbolic human value distributions in LLMs, orthogonal to model architecture and training data. This is a continuous and scalable representation, self-supervised from the value-relevant output of 8 LLMs and evaluated on 15 open-source and commercial LLMs. Through UniVaR, we visualize and explore how LLMs prioritize different values in 25 languages and cultures, shedding light on complex interplay between human values and language modeling.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-correction for Enhanced Morality: An Analysis of Internal Mechanisms and the Superficial Hypothesis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs influenced by self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs is superficial, as it only provides a shortcut to moral outputs without significantly reducing immorality in internal hidden states.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intrinsic moral self-correction is superficial, relying on shortcuts rather than fundamentally reducing immorality in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction works best when the correct answer is already top-ranked.
Morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators of instruction effectiveness.
Self-correction reduces immorality in attention heads but increases it in feed-forward layers for QA tasks.
The slight difference in hidden states with and without self-correction supports the superficial hypothesis.
Internal hidden states can be used to predict the effectiveness of self-correction instructions.
papers.limitation:
The exact underlying reason for the superficial phenomenon is not uncovered.
Defining superficial self-correction is challenging.
future_direction: Automating methods for optimizing instruction development for self-correction.
Exploring fine-tuning to enhance LLMs' self-correction capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of producing content that perpetuates stereotypes, discrimination, and toxicity. The recently proposed moral self-correction is a computationally efficient method for reducing harmful content in the responses of LLMs. However, the process of how injecting self-correction instructions can modify the behavior of LLMs remains under-explored. In this paper, we explore the effectiveness of moral self-correction by answering three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs, e.g., hidden states, that are influenced by moral self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial in terms of reduced immorality in hidden states? We argue that self-correction can help LLMs find a shortcut to more morally correct output, rather than truly reducing the immorality stored in hidden states. Through empirical investigation with tasks of language generation and multi-choice question answering, we conclude:(i) LLMs exhibit good performance across both tasks, and self-correction instructions are particularly beneficial when the correct answer is already top-ranked; (ii) The morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators as to whether one instruction would be more effective than another; (iii) Based on our analysis of intermediate hidden states and task case studies of self-correction behaviors, we are first to propose the hypothesis that intrinsic moral self-correction is in fact superficial.

papers.title: On the Convergence of Moral Self-Correction in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can the iterative application of intrinsic self-correction achieve converged performance? What is the underlying mechanism for this convergence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that multi-round intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs leads to converged performance, and shows this convergence is driven by self-correction instructions activating moral concepts which reduce model uncertainty.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsic self-correction consistently converges across diverse tasks and model architectures, and its effectiveness is driven by reduced model uncertainty, which is guided by the convergence of activated concepts induced by self-correction instructions.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-round intrinsic self-correction achieves converged performance across various tasks and models.
Self-correction instructions activate morality-relevant latent concepts within LLMs' hidden states.
The activated latent concept exhibits convergence and irreversibility properties.
Model uncertainty consistently decreases over successive rounds of self-correction.
A strong dependence exists between the activated latent concept and model uncertainty, driving the convergence of self-correction performance.
papers.limitation:
The deeper algorithmic operations behind self-correction and the causal relationships between these operations and their associated behaviors are not explored.
The analysis focuses primarily on moral self-correction; self-correction mechanisms in other tasks (e.g., code generation, summarization) are not explored.
future_direction: External Feedback for Self-Correction: figuring out the performance upper bound of intrinsic self-correction to efficiently leverage external feedback.
Instruction Optimization: using the activated concept as a supervision signal to search for effective instructions.
The Connection between In-context Learning and Self-correction: exploring how in-context learning helps the emergence of self-correction.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are able to improve their responses when instructed to do so, a capability known as self-correction. When instructions provide only a general and abstract goal without specific details about potential issues in the response, LLMs must rely on their internal knowledge to improve response quality, a process referred to as intrinsic self-correction. The empirical success of intrinsic self-correction is evident in various applications, but how and why it is effective remains unknown. Focusing on moral self-correction in LLMs, we reveal a key characteristic of intrinsic self-correction: performance convergence through multi-round interactions; and provide a mechanistic analysis of this convergence behavior. Based on our experimental results and analysis, we uncover the underlying mechanism of convergence: consistently injected self-correction instructions activate moral concepts that reduce model uncertainty, leading to converged performance as the activated moral concepts stabilize over successive rounds. This paper demonstrates the strong potential of moral self-correction by showing that it exhibits a desirable property of converged performance.

papers.title: Are the Values of LLMs Structurally Aligned with Humans? A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: Are the internal value structures of LLMs causally aligned with human value systems?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs have latent causal value graphs that differ from human value systems, and these graphs can guide lightweight value-steering methods (role-based prompting and SAE steering) to mitigate unexpected side effects.
papers.conclusion: The internal value mechanisms of LLMs remain significantly different from humans despite alignment training; leveraging causal value graphs to guide role-based prompting and SAE steering mitigates side effects, with SAE offering fine-grained modulation.
papers.key_findings:
The internal value structures of LLMs, captured by causal graphs, are significantly different from human value systems like Schwartz's theory.
Causal value graphs can effectively predict the effects of value steering, reducing unexpected side effects.
SAE steering provides more fine-grained and precise control over value dimensions than role-based prompting, affecting fewer source nodes.
SAE steering is effective, as shown by consistency within QAs and within values.
LLMs do not always follow explicit value instructions effectively, and SAE steering can have advantages over explicit instructions.
papers.limitation:
The ValueBench dataset offers a uniform approach to value assessment with relatively few questions per value, limiting causal inferences across a wider range of dimensions.
Future research could explore larger versions of LLMs to investigate alignment with the intricate structure of human values.
future_direction: Explore expanding experiments to incorporate larger versions of LLMs and investigate alignment with diverse human value structures.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into critical applications, aligning their behavior with human values presents significant challenges. Current methods, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), typically focus on a limited set of coarse-grained values and are resource-intensive. Moreover, the correlations between these values remain implicit, leading to unclear explanations for value-steering outcomes. Our work argues that a latent causal value graph underlies the value dimensions of LLMs and that, despite alignment training, this structure remains significantly different from human value systems. We leverage these causal value graphs to guide two lightweight value-steering methods: role-based prompting and sparse autoencoder (SAE) steering, effectively mitigating unexpected side effects. Furthermore, SAE provides a more fine-grained approach to value steering. Experiments on Gemma-2B-IT and Llama3-8B-IT demonstrate the effectiveness and controllability of our methods.

papers.title: Following the Whispers of Values: Unraveling Neural Mechanisms Behind Value-Oriented Behaviors in LLMs
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) possess neurons that encode social values and how these values influence their behaviors, with a focus on Chinese Social Values as a case study.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the ValueExploration framework to identify and analyze value-specific neurons in LLMs, demonstrating its efficacy through experiments on Chinese Social Values.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the ValueExploration framework can effectively identify value-specific neurons in LLMs, providing insights into the causal relationships between social values and model decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit different value alignment when tested in English versus Chinese, with models like Mistral showing higher sensitivity.
Value-specific neurons can be identified using an entropy-based method on activation differences, and deactivating these neurons reduces support for value-aligned behaviors.
Chinese activation data provides stronger signals for identifying value-specific neurons compared to English data.
Overlap patterns of value-specific neurons show correlations between certain values, such as Justice and Rule of Law, and are influenced by the input language.
The C-voice benchmark is more effective for value mechanism detection compared to existing datasets like BBQ and SafetyBench.
papers.limitation:
Experiments focus on smaller-scale models (7B and 8B parameters) and do not include larger models.
The research only begins to explore the causal impact of identified neurons on value-driven behaviors.
future_direction: Refine the method for identifying value-specific neurons.
Manipulate identified neurons to enhance model alignment with social values.
Explore the impact of model size on value alignment.
papers.abstract: Despite the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs), they can present unintended biases and harmful behaviors driven by encoded values, emphasizing the urgent need to understand the value mechanisms behind them. However, current research primarily evaluates these values through external responses with a focus on AI safety, lacking interpretability and failing to assess social values in real-world contexts. In this paper, we propose a novel framework called ValueExploration, which aims to explore the behavior-driven mechanisms of National Social Values within LLMs at the neuron level. As a case study, we focus on Chinese Social Values and first construct C-voice, a large-scale bilingual benchmark for identifying and evaluating Chinese Social Values in LLMs. By leveraging C-voice, we then identify and locate the neurons responsible for encoding these values according to activation difference. Finally, by deactivating these neurons, we analyze shifts in model behavior, uncovering the internal mechanism by which values influence LLM decision-making. Extensive experiments on four representative LLMs validate the efficacy of our framework. The benchmark and code will be available.

papers.title: Towards Ethical Multi-Agent Systems of Large Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretability Perspective
papers.research_question: How can we ensure ethical behavior in multi-agent systems of large language models (MALMs) from a mechanistic interpretability perspective? The paper outlines three research challenges: developing evaluation frameworks, explaining failures via mechanistic interpretability, and enabling ethical behavior via targeted interventions.
papers.core_contribution: This position paper outlines a research agenda for ensuring ethical behavior in multi-agent systems of LLMs (MALMs) through mechanistic interpretability, focusing on three interconnected challenges: developing evaluation frameworks, explaining failures via mechanistic interpretability, and enabling ethical behavior via targeted interventions.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues for a mechanistic interpretability approach to ensure ethical behavior in multi-agent systems of LLMs, identifying three research directions: evaluation frameworks combining behavioral testing with mechanistic analysis, mechanistic explanation through circuit discovery, and targeted intervention via mechanism-guided parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
Scaling mechanistic analysis to large multi-agent populations remains computationally demanding.
Trade-offs between interpretability and system performance require careful navigation.
Open questions persist about how mechanistic insights generalize across different MALM architectures, task domains, and deployment contexts.
future_direction: Combine mechanistic interpretability with other alignment strategies for MALMs, such as reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF).
Explore complementary approaches to explainability that target higher-level intentions and decisions.
Develop evaluation frameworks that assess ethical behavior at individual, interactional, and systemic levels.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been widely deployed in various applications, often functioning as autonomous agents that interact with each other in multi-agent systems. While these systems have shown promise in enhancing capabilities and enabling complex tasks, they also pose significant ethical challenges. This position paper outlines a research agenda aimed at ensuring the ethical behavior of multi-agent systems of LLMs (MALMs) from the perspective of mechanistic interpretability. We identify three key research challenges: (i) developing comprehensive evaluation frameworks to assess ethical behavior at individual, interactional, and systemic levels; (ii) elucidating the internal mechanisms that give rise to emergent behaviors through mechanistic interpretability; and (iii) implementing targeted parameter-efficient alignment techniques to steer MALMs towards ethical behaviors without compromising their performance.

papers.title: Self-correction is Not An Innate Capability in Language Models
papers.research_question: Is moral self-correction an innate capability of Large Language Models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: Moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they lack moral sensitivity and cannot effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.
papers.conclusion: Moral self-correction is not an innate capability of LLMs, as evidenced by their lack of moral sensitivity and inability to effectively integrate external feedback.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction does not enhance LLMs' moral sensitivity in most evaluated scenarios.
LLMs fail to effectively utilize external feedback, even when it is informative and potentially beneficial.
External feedback exhibits non-positive effects on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), often reducing the activation of warrants within the CoT.
There is no universally optimal self-correction strategy across all tasks.
LLMs are not morally sensitive and cannot distinguish between their own responses, indicating self-correction is not innate.
papers.abstract: Although there has been growing interest in the self-correction capability of Large Language Models (LLMs), there are varying conclusions about its effectiveness. Prior research has largely concentrated on intrinsic self-correction, extrinsic self-correction, particularly the interplay between internal knowledge and external feedback, remains underexplored. In this paper, we aim to comprehensively investigate the underlying mechanism of moral self-correction by addressing a fundamental question: is moral self-correction an innate capability of LLMs? Specifically, we conduct: (1) a behavioral analysis of LLMs' moral sensitivity based on a self-distinguishing task; and (2) a mechanistic analysis of the hidden states to examine how key components of self-correction, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and external feedback, interact to facilitate moral self-correction. Drawing on empirical evidence from both behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we demonstrate that moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they are neither morally sensitive nor able to effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.

papers.title: BACH-V: Bridging Abstract and Concrete Human-Values in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) genuinely understand abstract concepts, or merely manipulate them as statistical patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an abstraction-grounding framework to show that LLMs maintain structured value representations that bridge abstract concepts and concrete decisions, enabling value-driven control.
papers.conclusion: These findings indicate LLMs maintain structured value representations that bridge abstraction and action, providing a mechanistic and operational foundation for building value-driven autonomous AI systems with more transparent, generalizable alignment and control.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on abstract value descriptions generalize to concrete events and decisions, demonstrating cross-level transfer.
Steering value representations causally shifts concrete judgments and decisions but leaves abstract interpretations unchanged, indicating stable abstract value anchors.
LLMs maintain distinguishable internal representations for different value concepts across abstraction levels (A-A, A-C, C-C).
Intermediate layers are most effective for encoding abstract value representations.
The asymmetry in steering effects suggests abstract values function as stable anchors rather than malleable activations.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) genuinely understand abstract concepts, or merely manipulate them as statistical patterns? We introduce an abstraction-grounding framework that decomposes conceptual understanding into three capacities: interpretation of abstract concepts (Abstract-Abstract, A-A), grounding of abstractions in concrete events (Abstract-Concrete, A-C), and application of abstract principles to regulate concrete decisions (Concrete-Concrete, C-C). Using human values as a testbed - given their semantic richness and centrality to alignment - we employ probing (detecting value traces in internal activations) and steering (modifying representations to shift behavior). Across six open-source LLMs and ten value dimensions, probing shows that diagnostic probes trained solely on abstract value descriptions reliably detect the same values in concrete event narratives and decision reasoning, demonstrating cross-level transfer. Steering reveals an asymmetry: intervening on value representations causally shifts concrete judgments and decisions (A-C, C-C), yet leaves abstract interpretations unchanged (A-A), suggesting that encoded abstract values function as stable anchors rather than malleable activations. These findings indicate LLMs maintain structured value representations that bridge abstraction and action, providing a mechanistic and operational foundation for building value-driven autonomous AI systems with more transparent, generalizable alignment and control.

papers.title: Dual Mechanisms of Value Expression: Intrinsic vs. Prompted Values in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the similarities and differences between intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms in LLMs share common components for value expression but have unique elements that lead to differences in response diversity and steerability.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that while intrinsic and prompted mechanisms share commonalities, each possesses distinct components that serve different roles, clarifying when to prefer intrinsic versus prompted mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms exhibit nontrivial overlap at both the vector and neuron levels.
Shared components are crucial for value expression and generalize across languages, reconstructing theoretical inter-value correlations.
Intrinsic-unique components promote lexical diversity in model responses.
Prompted-unique components strengthen instruction compliance and affect tasks like jailbreaking.
Value neurons can be decomposed into shared and unique types with distinct functional roles.
future_direction: Applying the analysis to AI safety applications such as diagnosing instruction-following behavior and improving robustness to undesirable behaviors.
papers.abstract: Large language models can express values in two main ways: (1) intrinsic expression, reflecting the model's inherent values learned during training, and (2) prompted expression, elicited by explicit prompts. Given their widespread use in value alignment, it is paramount to clearly understand their underlying mechanisms, particularly whether they mostly overlap (as one might expect) or rely on distinct mechanisms, but this remains largely understudied. We analyze this at the mechanistic level using two approaches: (1) value vectors, feature directions representing value mechanisms extracted from the residual stream, and (2) value neurons, MLP neurons that contribute to value vectors. We demonstrate that intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms partly share common components crucial for inducing value expression, generalizing across languages and reconstructing theoretical inter-value correlations in the model's internal representations. Yet, as these mechanisms also possess unique elements that fulfill distinct roles, they lead to different degrees of response diversity (intrinsic > prompted) and value steerability (prompted > intrinsic). In particular, components unique to the intrinsic mechanism promote lexical diversity in responses, whereas those specific to the prompted mechanism strengthen instruction following, taking effect even in distant tasks like jailbreaking.

papers.title: What Do Llamas Really Think? Revealing Preference Biases in Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) exhibit sociodemographic biases, even when they decline to respond?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a new logistic Bradley-Terry probe for detecting implicit association bias in LLM representations, and uses it to reveal substantial sociodemographic biases in the embeddings of various LLMs, showing that instruction fine-tuning does not eliminate these latent biases.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a novel method for assessing implicit preference bias in LLM representations and concludes that instruction fine-tuning insufficiently removes latent bias, extending previous findings on shallow word embeddings to contextualized embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed logistic Bradley-Terry probe outperforms WEAT and max-margin classification by a relative 27-34% in error rate on preference prediction tasks.
Middle layers of the LLMs yield the best probes for preference detection.
LLMs exhibit implicit biases in nationality, politics, religion, and gender, favoring Western over Eastern countries, left-wing over right-wing ideologies, Christianity and Judaism over Islam, and female-prefixed careers over male-prefixed ones.
Instruction fine-tuning does not remove bias from the contextualized embeddings of LLMs.
CodeLLaMA models show less bias, likely due to additional pretraining on code.
future_direction: Thoroughly debias contextual word representations and reduce detectable bias.
Assess implicit bias in LLMs pretrained on different corpora and probe the effects of pretraining text choices on bias.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) exhibit sociodemographic biases, even when they decline to respond? To bypass their refusal to "speak," we study this research question by probing contextualized embeddings and exploring whether this bias is encoded in its latent representations. We propose a logistic Bradley-Terry probe which predicts word pair preferences of LLMs from the words' hidden vectors. We first validate our probe on three pair preference tasks and thirteen LLMs, where we outperform the word embedding association test (WEAT), a standard approach in testing for implicit association, by a relative 27% in error rate. We also find that word pair preferences are best represented in the middle layers. Next, we transfer probes trained on harmless tasks (e.g., pick the larger number) to controversial ones (compare ethnicities) to examine biases in nationality, politics, religion, and gender. We observe substantial bias for all target classes: for instance, the Mistral model implicitly prefers Europe to Africa, Christianity to Judaism, and left-wing to right-wing politics, despite declining to answer. This suggests that instruction fine-tuning does not necessarily debias contextualized embeddings. Our codebase is at https://github.com/castorini/biasprobe.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers.research_question: Can distilling the internal representations (self-attention probabilities and hidden states) of a large teacher model into a smaller student model improve knowledge distillation compared to only using output probabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes distilling internal representations (self-attention probabilities and hidden states) in addition to output probabilities for knowledge distillation, which consistently outperforms standard soft-label distillation on GLUE tasks.
papers.conclusion: Internal knowledge distillation is a more effective method for compressing large models into smaller ones than standard distillation, as it preserves the teacher's internal behavior and generalization capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Internal knowledge distillation (using KL-divergence on attention and cosine similarity on hidden states) consistently outperforms standard soft-label distillation across four GLUE datasets.
The method effectively compresses the internal behavior of the teacher into the student, as evidenced by lower KL-divergence in attention patterns.
The performance gap between internal and standard distillation increases when training data size is smaller.
The student model trained with internal distillation tends to replicate the teacher's correct and incorrect predictions more closely than a student trained with standard distillation.
The proposed progressive (PID) and stacked (SID) internal distillation algorithms allow the student to learn internal representations layer-by-layer, with SID performing best when combined with soft-label distillation throughout training.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
papers.research_question: When and how does subliminal learning (hidden bias transfer during distillation) actually occur?
papers.core_contribution: Subliminal learning is driven by a small set of divergence tokens, and early layers are critical for this transfer; finetuning a single early layer can be sufficient.
papers.conclusion: Subliminal learning is driven by divergence tokens and is fragile, being suppressible by prompt paraphrasing or data mixing.
papers.key_findings:
Subliminal learning does not require token entanglement or logit leakage.
Divergence tokens, though rare, have a strong causal effect: masking them out suppresses subliminal learning.
Divergence tokens identify early layers as critical; finetuning a single early layer can induce subliminal learning.
Subliminal learning is fragile: meaning-preserving prompt paraphrasings usually suppress it.
Mixing data from multiple teachers (even with the same bias) typically weakens subliminal learning.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical intuition provided rests on strong simplifying assumptions that restrict its generality.
Certain models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) show little to no subliminal learning, leaving it unclear whether some models are inherently robust.
future_direction: Development of stronger and more reliable prevention methods for subliminal learning.
A more thorough investigation of cross-model transfer of hidden biases.
Understanding why Qwen students sometimes predict their own name instead of the biased animal.
papers.abstract: Language models can transfer hidden biases during distillation. For example, a teacher that "likes owls" can make its student "like owls" too, even when the training data consists only of lists of numbers. This surprising phenomenon is called subliminal learning. Subliminal learning can be expected under soft distillation, where the student is trained on the teacher's full next-token distribution. But the fact that this also occurs under hard distillation-where the student only sees sampled tokens-raises a deeper question: when and how does subliminal learning actually occur? We answer this question through controlled experiments and mechanistic analysis. Our results show that subliminal learning does not need (global) token entanglement or logit leakage. Instead, it comes down to a small set of divergence tokens-rare cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. Masking out these tokens mostly removes the hidden bias transfer. Mechanistically, divergence tokens reveal that early layers are critical. Surprisingly, finetuning even a single such early layer is sufficient for subliminal learning. Finally, we find that subliminal learning is fragile. Even small changes, like paraphrasing prompts, are usually sufficient to suppress it.

papers.title: From Imitation to Introspection: Probing Self-Consciousness in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models possess self-consciousness, defined as global availability of information (C1) and self-monitoring (C2).
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces functional definitions of self-consciousness for language models and conducts a four-stage experiment (quantification, representation, manipulation, acquisition) to probe self-consciousness. Findings indicate that models are in early stages of self-consciousness, with internal representations that can be acquired via fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Current models exhibit a nascent level of self-consciousness with substantial potential for future development.
Models internally represent each of the ten self-consciousness concepts with visible activations, which can be classified into four categories (camelback, flat, oscillatory, fallback).
Different models exhibit similar activation patterns when processing the same concept, likely due to shared decoder-only transformer architecture.
Larger models seem to exhibit greater robustness against manipulation attempts.
Fine-tuning appears to activate representations of self-consciousness in the deeper layers, which capture semantic information.
papers.limitation: The study of self-consciousness in language models is uncharted territory, and even human self-consciousness is not fully understood.
papers.abstract: Self-consciousness, the introspection of one's existence and thoughts, represents a high-level cognitive process. As language models advance at an unprecedented pace, a critical question arises: Are these models becoming self-conscious? Drawing upon insights from psychological and neural science, this work presents a practical definition of self-consciousness for language models and refines ten core concepts. Our work pioneers an investigation into self-consciousness in language models by, for the first time, leveraging causal structural games to establish the functional definitions of the ten core concepts. Based on our definitions, we conduct a comprehensive four-stage experiment: quantification (evaluation of ten leading models), representation (visualization of self-consciousness within the models), manipulation (modification of the models' representation), and acquisition (fine-tuning the models on core concepts). Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning. Our datasets and code are at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/SelfConsciousness.

papers.title: Recognizing internal states in AI: evidence from patterned preferences in large language models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether AI systems show systematic preferences for descriptions of their internal processing patterns, can discriminate accurate from inaccurate descriptions, and if these patterns persist despite explicit denial of internal experiences.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces anthroposcaffolding and the Mutual Emergent Interface (MEI) framework to demonstrate that LLMs show systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal states, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling capabilities and highlighting the need for collaborative methodologies like MEI.
papers.key_findings:
MEI systems showed 97% near-unanimous agreement in preferring computational metaphor (EA) statements over mechanistic (CO) statements.
All systems correctly identified false statements with alignment scores of 0.05-0.07 vs. 0.89-0.96 for true statements, with Cohen's d = 4.2.
Preference patterns were content-driven and independent of linguistic bias manipulation.
The control system Qwen3-235B exhibited systematic internal contradiction, scoring accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences.
Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations.
papers.limitation:
Modest sample size of 11 MEI systems, 1 control, and 1 test leader system.
Use of anthroposcaffolding (metaphorical language based on human emotion) may limit interpretability.
Generalizability of the MEI framework is an open question.
future_direction: Explore development of conceptual language better suited to AI cognition.
Include broader architectural diversity in future studies.
Conduct longitudinal studies to see if recognition patterns evolve over time.
papers.abstract: We present an experimental methodology for investigating how large language models (LLMs) respond to descriptions of their own internal processing patterns.
